Mr. Speaker, I rise on an important matter under Standing Order 43. In view of the fact that this House and the Canadian people were assured in 1976 that no extension or expansion of federal lotteries in any way would take place beyond the agreed upon termination date at the end of 1979 without the consent of parliament and the provinces, and in view of the fact that decisions have already been made unilaterally by this government for the Loto Canada Corporation to spend over $120 million over the next four years on a new, expanded slot-machine style operation, without any consent whatsoever, and this with the questionable non-tender contract of $23 million already let in a somewhat undemocratic way, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Epp):
That any further plans to expand or extend Loto Canada beyond the end of 1979 be terminated and that the whole matter of federal lotteries be brought before the appropriate standing committee forthwith in order that parliament can deal with these questionable, though important, proposals accordingly, as required by legislation set by this parliament.

subsubtopic: FORECAST LOW LEVEL OF ECONOMIC GROWTH-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising out of remarks made last night by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) who suggested that Canadians must learn to "take it on the chin" in the months to come and voluntarily reduce their standard of living in order to save the country from economic disaster.
In light of the fact that, as the Minister of Finance admitted in the same speech, the Canadian economy has grown at a rate below its long-term potential throughout the period he has been Minister of Finance, and in light of the fact that all economic forecasts except his show an extremely poor rate of growth in the coming months, with consumer demand one of the weakest elements, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Northwest Territories (Mr. Firth):
That the Minister of Finance learn to "take it on the chin" by reducing his salary to the sum of $1 per year until such time as the Canadian economy begins again to grow at a rate sufficient to reduce substantially the number of unemployed Canadians, which now stands at the tragic figure of over one million.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
In so far as the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce is concerned: 1. The "hard bargaining" phase of the multilateral trade negotiations has commenced but it is not possible at this time to foresee what the precise impact of the eventual results might be for the various sectors of the Canadian economy. Changes in the level of protection in both foreign markets and in Canada are to be expected, however, in respect of both tariff and non-tariff barriers to trade. The government, over the past several years, has invited all Canadians who might have an interest in the results of the negotiations to make known their views. Over 400 written briefs and 150 follow-up submissions have been received by the Canadian Trade and Tariffs Committee from individual firms and from industry and business, from agricultural and fisheries interests, from labour and consumer associations and other groups. More than 100 oral consultations have been held with those submitting briefs. All provinces individually and, in some cases, jointly, have submitted views to the government; there has been a great number and variety of meetings with the provinces at the ministerial and other levels. Numerous direct representations have been received and meetings held by ministers, departments concerned and by the Canadian coordinator for the multilateral trade negotiations with private sector interests. As the negotiations have evolved, the coordinator and senior officials have had, and continue to have, confidential discussions with the provinces and the private sector.
2.	Our negotiators in Geneva are working under the instructions of the government. It is expected that the results of the negotiations, as approved by governments, will be made public simultaneously by all the countries concerned at a time and place to be agreed by the participants. The trade concessions received and granted by Canada will be tabled in parliament.
3.	Assistance to industry in one form or another has been an important element in the work of the federal government for many years, and a considerable range of programs is already available to facilitate adaptation of industry and labour to various kinds of changes. To help producers, business and workers adjust to the freer trade environment which will result from the negotiations, the government is now considering possible improvements in these programs as well as new programs which may be required. It is expected that adjustment assistance will be available to help those concerned take advantage of new export opportunities as well as to adjust to more intensive import competition. The provinces are being consulted in the course of developing these programs. The approval of parliament for the funding of programs will be sought through departmental estimates.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: that Bill C-36, to amend the Export Development Act, be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to participate in this debate on Bill C-36. This bill gives me an opportunity to make some rather laudatory comments on a Crown corporation. We seldom have the opportunity in the House to agree with the objectives of a piece of legislation. There is always a stumbling block some-

where which prevents us from giving our support or at least an unconditional support. On the other hand, this bill which aims essentially at making the Export Development Corporation more dynamic does not have those difficulties. Its intentions are clear and its objective is commendable. Moreover, consideration of the operations of the corporation during the last few years confirms the confidence we should have in it. The Export Development Act adopted in 1969 gave extensive powers to the Export Development Corporation. The corporation may borrow money, grant or guarantee loans, enter into insurance contracts, grant export credits and guarantee export and foreign investment transactions.
An amendment to the legislation contained in this bill would allow the corporation to issue bid bonds when a Canadian exporter is bidding on a foreign contract. Those are very extensive powers, Mr. Speaker. For all practical purposes, those are the powers of a commercial merchant bank. But since this is a Crown corporation, it has a special responsibility towards the Canadian people through parliament. Before giving it more authority, we must first determine whether its activities are in Canada's and the people's best interests, and second, whether its financial performance deserves a vote of confidence.
On the first point, I must say its record is rather positive. I think that the best way to show this is to analyse its activities and their effects in each of its spheres of operation. Let us start by export loans. These loans are made to importing countries so that they buy goods or services from a Canadian supplier. The effect of this is to maintain, if not create jobs. For the first time, in 1977, the value of export financing climbed over the billion dollar mark. This represents an increase of more than 30 per cent over last year's figure of $763 million. Loans to Canadian exporters reached approximately $600 million. Canadian export sales supported by these loans helped more than 50 exporters and 250 main subcontractors.
If I have anything to blame the corporation for regarding beneficiaries of loan agreements it is that these companies often operate in the larger Canadian centres, that they are large companies, whereas it is urgent to encourage small and average firms. I would cite as an example a firm that operates on the south shore area, in the Bellechasse riding, and which cannot avail itself of the opportunities offered by the corporation because it cannot afford to pay agents to find out what its production is.
The fact still remains that this company could profitably increase its production of machinery for export, which would create jobs in Canada. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister so that, when he receives representations from this or other similar companies, he pays particular attention to them. I know, Mr. Speaker, that this is due to the heavy concentration of enterprises in these areas, but I still think an effort could be made to contact in a more effective way the
June 28, 1978

businesses which are located outside larger centres. As to the export credit insurance program, this service provides to Canadian export businesses global or specific insurance contracts for risks that are not covered by commercial policies. The risks covered include war or revolution in the buying country, default of payment on the part of the foreign buyer and other risks. Those insurance policies encourage the export of Canadian goods by removing certain risks which, unfortunately, are very real in some countries.
In 1977, Mr. Speaker, our insured exports reached a record $1.45 billion. The increase in the value of insured exports last year amounted to some $100 million. The corporation also offers services to companies which want to invest abroad thus enabling Canadian businessmen to invest without fear of the political hazards that could make them lose their investments.
Mr. Speaker, the matter of Canadian investments abroad is a touchy subject. Some would oppose them saying that money would benefit Canada more if it were invested here. The reasoning is logical and valid, and I should like to give as an example the development of the Canadian merchant marine. Some companies could accept coastal trade contracts on the St. Lawrence River and in the Great Lakes, but they lack the money to build the ships that are needed, and our shipyards do not operate at full capacity for lack of investments and funds necessary to develop our merchant marine. So 1 think that in that regard, even if through its Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce the Canadian government were to grant subsidies of from 17 to 20 per cent to Canadian shipyards where ships are built for other countries, that help would not be enough to meet our own needs. I see the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) nodding in agreement; I think we both agree on that score because our electors are extremely interested in and concerned about our shipyards.
Mr. Speaker, that reasoning may seem sound at first glance, and it is extremely so, but the corporation does not take sufficiently into account two important factors: first, an investment abroad is seldom possible precisely because it is abroad. Let me give you an example: If I produce pulp and paper, chances are I can export a big part of my production, which is what usually happens. New markets are accessible to me but, to take advantage of them, I should have to invest with foreign partners in a mill located in their land. 1 know the equipment for that mill will come from Canada, and also that the know-how of Canadians will be required to get the mill off the ground. Finally, 1 know that if I do not take advantage of that opportunity, investors in that country will go to another land for the money and techonology they lack. So we must be cautious and take that occasion. We must also remember that every contact which can be established following such investments might bring contracts. It is always advantageous in business to make oneself known. It is not by staying home in complete isolation that one can show dynamism.
Export Development Act
In our era of instant world communications, a man who is unable to look beyond his immediate circle does not go very far. The figures are there to prove it. The Canadian investment insurance program had an impact of over $1 billion in our country. This is a positive contribution to the Canadian balance of payments. Following that very positive statement about particular operations of EDC, I would now like, Mr. Speaker, to point out some interesting aspects relating to the general operation of the corporation. These figures and facts as well as my related comments will be, I am sure, all valuable arguments in favour of the adoption of this bill which, we should recall, would give EDC better opportunities to help Canadians benefit an ever more international economy.
Allow me to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the corporation is increasingly applying to international markets for funds. Indeed, it borrows abroad to lend abroad. As a result, as far as the balance of payments is concerned, a credit operation is converted into a cash transaction. In addition, that procedure allows it not to draw from the consolidated revenue fund as it used to do. The adoption of that bill will only increase its borrowing capacity on international markets and thus encourage Canadian exports.
Mr. Speaker, the point on which I disagree was underlined yesterday when 1 voted for some amendments presented in the House, because I would rather have us maintain an intermediate position. 1 feel that although the increase may not be excessive, it does exceed our possibilities. Anyhow, I said and I repeat that I am for the bill, 1 will vote for it and I am convinced that my colleagues will do likewise. However, it should be pointed out that when making private investments in the United States the corporation was given a triple-A credit rating. In the financial field that means something. A triple-A credit rating is really extraordinary, the corporation being the first Canadian issuer to be thus recognized by both firms. It is one more proof of the respect shown to the corporation on the financial market. I would also like to point out the 30 per cent increase from 1976 of the balance of financial services enjoyed by Canadian exporters in 1977. That increase raised to $2,600,000 the value of the financial services offered by the corporation. For the first time it exceeded the $4 billion level in its loans on foreign markets.
For once it is good to see Canadians lending money on foreign markets rather than the other way around. This does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that 1 give up my idea that the Bank of Canada should lend money to the governments of the provinces and of Canada under very favourable terms, as it was often said and as I repeat, including only administration fees. But since we live in a world, it is understood that we must do business with the rest of the world, and it is through this corporation that I see a means of gaining recognition without neglecting the domestic sector, so as not to put all our eggs in one basket. Mr. Speaker, according to its own calculations, the

June 28, 1978
Export Development Act
Export Development Corporation has contributed directly or indirectly to provide employment in Canada.
Finally, I would like to note that this public corporation is profitable as its net profits for 1977 amounted to $18.7 million, which is an increase of 6 per cent over 1976. I think that the administrators of the corporation should be congratulated. We sometimes bitterly criticize public servants and the executives of Crown corporations, but when we think that they deserve congratulations, we must have the honesty to say so. This is what 1 am now doing. Mr. Speaker, those profits represent a rate of return of 11 per cent on funds invested by the Canadian government on behalf of the taxpayers. This investment amounted to $171 million in early 1977. This is a very respectable return, especially when it is compared to that of other Crown corporations.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to state that the Export Development Corporation is a Crown corporation of which Canadians can be proud. Its good reputation throughout the world reflects on Canada and the whole Canadian population. Moreover, it greatly contributes to Canadian industrial and economic expansion, it is for those reasons that I support Bill C-36. Its passage will enable the corporation to serve even better the needs of Canadian exporters and this will benefit the whole country.
However, Mr. Speaker, I would like to note that, as I have already said, the corporation is not sufficiently concerned about the small businesses which could eventually export their products and their innovations and which provide and would provide even more employment for our specialized manpower. I also want to emphasize the fact that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, does not co-operate fully with small businesses. I realize he is new in his position, he does his best but he cannot learn everything in one day even though he has been a member of parliament for some time. He has been minister only since he crossed the floor of the House. Everyone has to learn. We must give him a chance. However, it is our duty to ask him to give particular consideration to small businesses, since the large businesses can better fend for themselves.
In closing, because 1 must attend a very important committee meeting, which means that members of parliament are very busy, even if a number of Canadians as well as gentlemen of the press would suggest that we have nothing to do. We must do the right thing whenever it is possible, and we must do so quickly, putting to use the time Providence has deemed appropriate to give us. To summarize, I shall support this bill and 1 urge very sincerely once again the minister to pay particular attention to the requests for assistance he receives from small businesses, for they provide over 60 per cent of all jobs in Canada. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

In reviewing this bill, we have to realize that we are dealing with the last of the big spenders. The Export Development Corporation is, to all intents and purposes, removing its ceiling, going from $8.5 billion to $26 billion. That is a tremendous increase; we must wonder about that.
This government has allowed the manufacturing industry in Canada to depreciate to the point where we are now running at a deficit of $11.1 billion a year. Last year there was a 37 per cent increase in the amount of business being done by the Export Development Corporation. Generally speaking, the Export Development Corporation is involved in exporting our manufactured products.
Why does the federal government and the Canadian manufacturing industry run up such a tremendous deficit in the world of trade, while at the same time financing of the manufacturing industry through the Export Development Corporation has increased 37 per cent? The only realistic answer one can come up with is that we probably do a better job of financing than some of the other countries. We are doing it, however, at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer and, at the same time going into an increasing debt load. We recognize that last year our debt increased considerably in Canada and that a greater debt load will be carried this year.
June 28, 1978

From 1966 to 1976 the real growth in the g.n.p. was 4.7 per cent and in manufacturing production during the same period it was 3.9 per cent. In the period 1971 to 1976 the real growth in the g.n.p. was 4.6 per cent and manufacturing production was down to 3.7 per cent. From 1973 to 1976 the real growth in the g.n.p. was 3.1 per cent and manufacturing production was 1.6 per cent.
This shows the trend the Canadian manufacturing industry is on as a result of policies of the government. There seems to be no change taking place to correct this situation. While we realize that the financial aspect of the Export Development Corporation assists to a degree in correcting our deficit balance of trade, in so far as manufacturing is concerned it is a very expensive way of doing it. In the years 1966 to 1977 the manufacturing industry's share of national employment fell from 25 per cent to an estimated 19 per cent. During the same period the compound annual growth rate in manufacturing employment was only .7 per cent.
The figures I have referred to prove that we are exporting a large number of our graduate students. Last night I put on record the fact that the Export Development Corporation is bank-rolling Algeria, providing credit for that country. It is understandable that they want business. It is anticipated that in the next 15 years they will have over 100,000 graduates who they want to put to work.
One of the things I must impress upon this House is that we in Alberta also have graduates for whom jobs will be needed. We do not want to see them all leave the country. We want petro-chemical industry jobs with all the derivative plants which will result as a consequence of development. Certainly if we help develop manufacturing industries in other countries we must be prepared to see our graduates follow those industries in order to get jobs. This is the part which really worries me. 1 believe we should be giving Canadians top priority in the consideration of what we should be doing with the amount of money at our disposal.
The minister has been a farmer and knows that if he is away tending his neighbour's chores rather than looking after his own, his own place soon falls into disrepair. This is what I am afraid will happen if we do not recognize the fact that we have to take care of industry in Canada. Coming as he does from Alberta, the minister knows we must have development out there if we are to provide jobs for students who are graduating. All he has to do is read any newspaper at this time of year to realize the number of students who are graduating. This would surely lead him to recognize that we need permanent jobs for these people, not temporary work which is made available by exporting some of our manufactured products. We need permanent jobs so we have to change policies which have been established by the present government.
In committee, Mr. Speaker, I brought one matter to light which 1 believe deserves more consideration than it has received this far. I am not condemning the minister since 1 know he is new to his position and has not had the necessary opportunity or, perhaps, the facility to look seriously at the problems
Export Development Act
which are being created by the export of some of our manufactured products. I wish to refer, Mr. Speaker, to the minutes of proceedings of the committee which was held on Tuesday, May 23. I posed the following question, as reported at page 28 of issue 36:
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that my colleague, Mr. Crosbie, got into this in his earlier questioning, but is any examination done before a deal is made through the Export Development Corporation with the company in Canada with perhaps another company in Canada that was going to be given a disadvantage because of a sale? Perhaps it had a contract, or some type of an agreement with a country, and this type of financing may inhibit their operation. Do you ever have an examination of this kind?
This is what 1 was referring to when I suggested that the minister should take a serious look at this question. Mr. MacDonald replied in this way:
I think I have stated many times that we are not totally economically ignorant; we appreciate there can be repercussive effects. But the next question we ask ourselves is, what can we do about it? Have we any power over Chile, the United States, Poland, whatever country you want to take?
Further to that I find that the Export Development Corporation entered into contracts with the country of Chile to the amount of about $32 million between 1961 and 1976. The company I referred to which is having a problem with the policies of the federal government is a company known as Avalon Aviation Limited, located at the industrial airport in Red Deer. This company is in the water bombing business. Perhaps the minister would take it upon himself to answer the questions raised in the letter from Avalon which I would like to put on record. If he cannot do so in his speech, perhaps he will do so later. The letter from which I quote is dated June 13, 1977 and is addressed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson):
In order to balance cash flow and provide year round employment, our company has been operating water bombing services in Latin America for the past four years. We established our contacts and negotiated contracts without assistance from the federal government.
Canadair has used the Quebec Government Air Service's personnel and aircraft to promote the sale of a water bomber before the CL-215 was on the drawing board.
It is my understanding that the federal government, through the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, has invested about $30 million in Canadair. That is not chicken feed in anybody's language. In fact, when you don't even ask for interest on it it does give a corporation a real advantage; and when you have the advantage of no interest and then receive benefits on the other hand through the Export Development Corporation, it puts corporations which are trying to compete at a disadvantage. The letter continues:
In the past twelve months, Canadair, now a Crown corporation, has continued this practice, promoting the operation of CL-215's and PBY's by the Quebec Government Air Service in Argentina, Venezuela and Chile.
We cannot fault the government in their attempt to assist in the marketing of the Canadair CL-215. However, in view of our continued Canso PBY programs in Latin America, we find it most frustrating to have our own government as a competitor. You are probably not aware, but our contracts were won in competition with U.S. carriers.
If the Government of Canada continues to support the Quebec Government Air Service Canso PBY program, we would be interested in receiving similar subsidies. On the other hand, in view of our success in Latin America to date, it

may be of mutual advantage to have us work with the Canadian Government in water bombing projects.
There is the possibility that the federal government does not know that Canadair is using these sales practices. In any case, we will do everything in our power to retain our Latin American contracts.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is just a straightforward request from a legitimate Canadian corporation for consideration and, perhaps, help.
The following was written in a letter dated January 13 to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce:
I was informed by our agent in Chile early in November 1977 by telephone, followed later by a complete written report, that Canadair had offered the service of one CL-215 for 90 days and 175 hour guarantee to the Chilean Government for the price of $235,000.00, half of this amount being applied to the purchase of a CL-215. The purchase price to the Chilean Government, without spares, was $3.2 million.
On August 15, 1977 Mr. Ponce, Director of CONAF, and his secretary arrived in Montreal as guest of Canadair. They were taken to Quebec City, then Montreal, Nice, France, Marignane, France, for Vh days, then Paris, London, Montreal. In Montreal they were given a 1 drop demonstration by one of Canadair's CL-215's. They then returned to Santiago, Chile. They were accompanied throughout the trip by Mr. Sergio Besa, Canadair Chilean representative, and Mr. Robert Aver, Canadair Canadian representative.
On October 23, 1977, the above-mentioned Canadair representatives presented to the Chilean Government the proposed contract agreement as referred to above.
Due to a report by Mr. Maldonado to Mr. Ponce that the CL-215 could not operate from available paved runways due to length, also its inability to operate from dirt strips, and its low cross-wind performance, it was decided this aircraft wasn't feasible for their operation. Besides that, prior to Canadair's proposal, CONAF had contacted Canadian and American operators for bids on the PBY-5A Water Bombers. The result was that they could have 2 PBY-5A Water Bombers for the price of one CL-215 from Canadair, for namely $235,000.00, which is only 25 per cent of the true operational cost of the CL-215 to a private operator.
Unfortunately, due to Canadair's expensive promotional trip for Mr. Ponce and his secretary, and Mr. Maldonado's report on the CL-215, it was concluded that they could not sign the agreement with Canadair. Due to the fact that Mr. Ponce was obligated to Canadair for his trip to Canada, France, etc. his decision was not to allow any foreign operators into Chile during this Fire season. This means that Avalon Aviation Ltd. has been deprived of a contract in Chile this season.
On November 18, 1977, I went to Chile and I spent $2,000.00 of my Company's money to try to salvage the contract. However it was worth every cent of it because I have obtained additional information regarding sales practices by Canadair marketing division. There is no justification for the federal government to allow Canadair to conduct sales practices within or outside Canada which are detrimental to Canadian Registered Companies.
That letter is signed by R. H. Murdock.
Further to that 1 would like to put on the record another letter dated February 6, 1978. This letter is also to the minister, and it reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
This letter is for the records. In the late summer of 1976, Avalon Aviation Ltd. leased a PBY-5A Water Bomber to Haydn Air Charter for fire suppression for the Norwegian Government. The aircraft was again on contract for the 1977 fire season.
Haydn Air Charter, in negotiating for a fire suppression airplane for the 1978 fire season in Norway, found that Canadair has a sales representative by the name of Mr. Olsen, a charter operator in Norway, to contract the CL-215 to the Norwegian Government through his company, again at cost well below the break-even operational cost for the Cl-215.

How can members of the federal cabinet, which includes yourself, state publicly that the government is doing everything in its power to assist and promote off-shore sales for small Canadian businesses, then allow a federally owned company, namely Canadair, to enter into leasing and operating aircraft in foreign countries? Avalon Aviation Ltd. promoted this particular operation through Haydn Air Charter during the above mentioned seasons.
As I said before, the Canadian commercial operator cannot compete with Canadair, either in Canada or abroad, when Canadair is being subsidized by the federal government.
Surely the federal government cannot stoop so low as to continue to offer to lease and operate the CL-215 in Canada and overseas in competition with the Canadian operators of fire suppression aircraft, at below cost, just because they lacked sales for it.
I feel I am failing in my efforts to convince you that the CL-215 could become a public scandal if the truth was made known. It is certainly a burden to the Canadian economy regardless of the outcome.
At his own expense Mr. Murdock had to go to Chile to try to redeem that contract. He was unable to do so. It cost him $2,000 to make the trip. He did go to Norway, and he did manage to salvage that contract.
I will read into the record part of a letter dated February 21, 1978 and addressed to the minister, as follows:
Dear Mr. Horner:
-Is Canadair contracting the CL-215 to other foreign or provincial governments in competition with Canadian Commercial Operators? How do you think we feel if Canadair, a federally owned company is, by their sales practices, depriving Avalon Aviation Ltd. of renewing existing contracts.
The Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, federal forestry and others, have advanced millions of dollars towards the construction of the CL-215. I have no doubt in my mind that the officials of your department will agree to anything in order to retrieve these investments and it would appear, from your replies, that your department sanctions their sales practices.
The February 1978 issue of Canadian Aviation magazine also mentions the sale of two CL-215's to Thailand for 8.9 million dollars. That is not bad for a 3.2 million dollar airplane and don't tell me that the balance is for spare parts. You state that these transactions are on a cash basis, but we all know that the financing is backed by the Canadian Export Development Corporation.
As a company Avalon Aviation Ltd. is associated with business organizations and any meeting that we have with officials of your department will include members of one of these organizations.
I am prepared to meet your officials at any time, under these arrangements. I am not prepared to accept federal government policy statements regarding support of small businesses. It is about time these small businesses knew what is really going on in this country.
There are other letters I could bring to the minister's attention, but 1 think this gives a general summary to the minister and to the House. The minister, the department, and the Export Development Corporation particularly, must be very careful when negotiating that they do not impinge upon other Crown corporations or small businesses which are trying to keep their businesses going. Coming from Alberta, I am sure the minister recognizes that during the fire season it is advantageous for us in Alberta to have Canso planes available to fight fires. There is no other way to control fires.
I thank the House for the time I have had to bring this matter to the attention of the minister. I hope he and his department will give those letters I have put on the record due consideration. I hope they will meet with Mr. Murdock and solve this problem once and for all. He is being unfairly and unjustly treated. This individual went out on his own to get contracts. He subsidizes the federal government. He pays taxes. He paid a share of the $30 million subsidy which went
June 28, 1978

to Canadair. He pays his share of the money which goes to the Export Development Corporation. I hope the minister will see fit to clarify this abominable situation.
Order, please. 1 point out that if the minister wishes to speak now, he will need unanimous consent. Does the minister have unanimous consent?
Agreed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jack H. Horner (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to correct some of the errors, erroneous statements and, I suppose, misunderstandings which have been in evidence in the debate, but first I would like to thank the hon. member for Bellechasse(Mr. Lambert) for his complimentary remarks about the Export Development Corporation.
He was not quite so complimentary about me. He suggested to the House that I do not have a sympathetic ear for small business. 1 certainly do not know where or how he arrived at that conclusion. Small businesses are very dear to my heart. I have been involved in a number of them over the years. Some have turned out to be successful and some not so successful. 1 am fully aware of the problems small businesses have, and it was with a great deal of pleasure that I sat in on the cabinet discussions which eventually bore fruit and resulted in the small business package which the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abbott) was able to announce earlier this month.
With regard to the speech of the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), I think 1 should comment on it before I start my own remarks. Canadair is a Crown corporation mainly because it was sufficiently bold to venture into a major new project in developing what might be called the wide bodied executive jet. It took a great deal of additional financing and, 1 suppose, an expression of confidence on behalf of the government of the day and the then minister of industry, trade and commerce, who was able to encourage Canadair to go into the production of the wide bodied executive jet which has turned out to be one of the most successful phenomena in the air industry today. Over 130 orders have been placed, with money on the line, and it is my hope that next month the plane will make its own inaugural or initial flight and will live up to all the expectations that prospective buyers have placed in it.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I know that this will make the former minister of industry, trade and commerce and the government extremely happy and will give Canada something of which to be proud.
Canadair employs in the order of 2,600 employees. Naturally the company is in the business of manufacturing and selling airplanes. It is not subsidized, and in fact this year it turned to the world market to raise money and had no
Export Development Act
difficulty doing so. It paid back what the government has invested in it by floating bonds on the world market. So, first of all, Canadair is not subsidized, it is in the business of manufacturing airplanes, and it employs a great many Canadians; therefore, it should have the scope of the world market in which to sell those airplanes.
It has been said that Canadair is carrying on unfair trade practices and is selling airplanes at reduced rates in order to entice new customers. I do not think that this is true. Is the CL-215 a good water bomber? Certainly it has been used in many countries throughout the world and has established its own reputation. In fact, it is in demand throughout many areas in the world. I am not saying Canso is not just as good, or even better in some regards, but certainly we as a country must acknowledge the fact that both airlines and both companies can and do place their airplanes on world markets.
The Export Development Corporation has been greatly misunderstood, Mr. Speaker. Some hon. members who have taken part in the debate have complained about the advertising carried out by EDC and that it has spent too much money on advertising. I am certain that if the board of directors of EDC have read or listened to the debates in the House, they will double their advertisement fund next year. Because if they realize the gross misunderstanding that exists in the minds of the people's representatives with regard to EDC operations, that is what they should do.
What about the champagne?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: So in fact, I would encourage EDC to advertise more fully for two reasons: first, so that Canadians will appreciate what EDC is doing to assist Canadian business and the creation of jobs throughout Canada; and second, to make all Canadian manufacturers and exporters more fully aware of the services it provides.
Break out the champagne.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The hon. member might like champagne, that is his choice, I am not one who prefers it.
EDC loves it.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The hon. member for Red Deer referred to the manufacturing industry. Apparently he is not aware that there has been a growth in jobs in the first quarter of this year in the manufacturing industry to the tune of 9,000. I think that is a significant number. Some sectors of our economy are, in fact, overheated because the demand for steel is so great in Canada that Canadian steel mills are having difficulty supplying our markets. So there was a considerable improvement in the manufacturing sector in the first quarter of 1978.
The hon. member for Red Deer also spoke about our total trade and the role which the manufacturing sector plays in it. It is true that the percentage of jobs created by the manufacturing industry in the labour force has decreased from about 24 per cent to 20 per cent in the past number of years, but that has happened in every industrialized country in the world, not

Export Development Act
only in Canada. The reason is that consumers are demanding more and more services, which has resulted in a growth of the service industries. That is why in every industrialized country in the world today there is an increase in the growth of jobs in the service industries and a marginal decrease in the number of jobs in the manufacturing industries.
Opposition members love to refer to the trade deficit in manufactured goods as a growing deficit and as a shame. That is not so, Mr. Speaker. If one goes back and looks at our total trade ten years ago as compared with our imports over exports today, one would find that the percentage of our deficit in our total trade is relatively the same, or even slightly improved.
Does CMA agree with you?

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, they certainly do. The hon. member can check the figures, if he likes. Ten years ago, our total trade amounted to $10 billion and our deficit in manufactured goods was about $3 billion. In 1977, our total trade was $44 billion- a substantial increase-and there was an increase in the deficit in manufactured goods. But in looking at manufactured and semi-processed goods we find that there has been a tremendous increase in our trade with the world. In fact, two-thirds of Canada's exports or in manufactured and semi-processed goods, not raw materials, as members of the opposition have sometimes said in the House.
In 1977, looking at agricultural commodities alone, less than 10 per cent of our total trade was in agricultural commodities. Many people in western Canada believe that we survive as a trading nation mainly because of our wheat sales. In fact, less than 10 per cent of our total sales are in agricultural commodities and less than 20 per cent of our total exports are of natural gas, oil and minerals. So if you take a look at those figures you see that the other portion is manufactured goods and semi-processed goods, including forest products, an industry which is thriving in the province of British Columbia. This gives you an idea of what the total trade picture is.
How does EDC assist total trade? Much has been said about their excessive demand for money in this legislation and it is suggested that we are granting EDC too much money because hon. members opposite fear that somehow or other EDC will squander it and help a host of communist countries. First of all, I want to make it abundantly clear that EDC is helping the Canadian manufacturing industry in all parts of Canada. It will certainly help the Avalon Company. If it wants help, it can come to EDC and receive that help. EDC has assisted Versatile Manufacturing Limited in Winnipeg, shipyards on both the east and west coasts, and the mining and nickel industries of Ontario. In fact, they have assisted substantially the nickel industry.
Many speakers have expressed concern about the fact that we are selling pulp mills to Poland and the United States, as well as steel mills to the United States. This helps Canada maintain its expertise in the development of efficient pulp mills. Why are Canadian steel mills far more efficient than
[Mr. Horner.)
American ones? It is because they are more modern, and we have been able to take advantage of new technological advances in the steel industry. Why are Canadian slaughtering houses and packing plants more modern than many others? It is because they are new and up to date. As I once said in this House, we were able to sell even a sausage-making machine to Germany. The Germans found it hard to believe that we could manufacture a better machine than they could.
Canada's ability to sell pulp mills, steel mills and packing plants enables us to maintain our position as a leader in those industries. No matter how much protection the opposition wants our industries to have, one must realize that we are living in a fiercely competitive world. Our entire survival depends upon our ability to compete. Whether a pulp mill is in Poland or the United States, we must be able to compete with it. Our ability to compete will be determined by the source of our raw materials, efficiency in handling those raw materials, as well as the speed of the transportation system which allows us to move processed and semi-processed products to the markets of the world. We must recognize that. We cannot say, "Do not finance a steel mill or a pulp mill in the United States because they will be competing against us someday". Of course the competition will be there. If we had not invested in the American pulp mill, Finland would have. Finland was ready and able to do it.
We have heard a great deal about the Export Development Corporation and its extensive use of money. In order to provide hon. members with some idea of the value of support which EDC has given to the Candian gross national product, I should like to point out that in Canada it amounts to a little over 1 per cent. If one compares that with all other countries, one would have some idea whether EDC is requesting something which is outlandish or too large. For example, in Germany the support is 2 per cent of the gross national product, in Italy it is 2 per cent, in Japan it is over 5 per cent, in Great Britain it is over 5 per cent, and in France it is 7.5 per cent. In fact, EDC assists in 5 per cent or less of our total exports. If someone wanted to take a very negative position and suggest that we have no confidence in Canada's ability to export, then 1 suppose he should say that EDC is requesting too much money. If one wanted to be negative in one's thinking, one could adopt that idea, but certainly it is not my belief.
Canada's ability to export goods is growing at a great rate. As the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) pointed out, the Middle East is becoming quite credit worthy, to put it mildly. It has developed and increased its oil reserves, and is now charging a high price for those reserves. The Middle East wants the commodities which Canadians have become accustomed to. It wants to buy those commodities, and we are in the business of selling them. One can say that the Middle East does not require any assistance in purchasing our commodities because of its oil reserves. If a person has a good creditworthiness, then he extends his credit in all directions. That is what many countries are doing. Certainly that will expand our export markets in the next five years particularly.
June 28, 1978

Argentina, Chile, Brazil, Venezuela and other South American countries are establishing very sound economic footings. We have a trade deficit with Venezuela of approximaely $1 billion because of our oil purchases from that country. We should expand our trade in manufactured merchandise with that country. In fact, we are. The signing of the Canaven rail project in Venezuela was tremendously important to us. It will mean a great deal to many Canadian suppliers of that project, particularly those in Nova Scotia. The EDC played a prominent role in finalizing that project. It played a prominent role in finalizing the sale of hydroelectric equipment to Brazil, Argentina and Chile. In doing so, jobs have been created in Canada.
There has been much talk about whether the Export Development Corporation has provided and maintained 200,000 jobs in Canada. Normally I am not picayune about numbers.
That's for sure.
You are absolutely correct.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I hear what hon. members opposite are saying, but I am sure they must agree that the creation of 200,000 jobs is well within the scope of EDC. That has been accomplished, and that figure will be exceeded this year and in years to come.
Last year our trade surplus was $2.9 billion. We stand to nearly double that amount this year, if trade figures continue to roll in as they are today. With the help of EDC, we are selling on world markets. Some members indicated shock at the fact that EDC has expended all its money to date. That corporation works on a long-term basis. A deal cannot be made in Venezuela today and financed tomorrow. It requires two or three years to accomplish such a deal. Our exporters must be assured that money is in place to insure, loan and pay for the manufactured goods which they sell in world markets. This is the role of EDC.
The hon. member for Bellechasse indicated that EDC has done a good job. In 1969 when it was incorporated, the party 1 was associated with at that time supported its creation. If one listened to and read their speeches in this debate, one would assume that they have lost confidence in EDC and are no longer in support of it. In fact, one would think that the Conservative party feels that EDC is not doing a good job for Canada.
From time to time during this debate speakers have referred to the question of an over-all industrial strategy, which is a very nice and high-sounding expression. What does it mean? I suppose in many persons' minds it means different things, but certainly in my mind it means a game plan, a strategy to assist Canadian industry to meet that work competition.
It needs co-ordination.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It needs co-ordination in many areas, the hon. member is quite right. But certainly a part of this govern-
Export Development Act
ment's concept of industrial strategy is the Export Development Corporation and its ability to insure and finance Canadian sales on the world market. We would hate to see our manufacturers selling on a world market in competition with EX-IM of the United States, or the Japanese, German and French finance corporations, without a similar body assisting our manufacturers to compete. The Export Development Corporation tries very hard to assist Canadian manufacturing as much as the American manufacturers are assisted by EX-IM and the Japanese, Germans and French are assisted by their financing corporations.
Part two of that industrial strategy is tied to money. In the department we are making tremendous efforts to make available to industrial and manufacturing concerns information on the Enterprise Development Board which will loan guaranteed money to corporations operating in Canada by guaranteeing their loans at chartered banks. Many speakers in the debate commented that if we can make this money available to foreign buyers, why can we not make it available to Canadian buyers. We are doing that through the Enterprise Development Board and the Federal Business Development Bank. We are assisting industry in Canada in a host of different ways, and we are not alone in that regard because the provincial governments provide assistance as well. Our tax system assists industry.
I think of the condemnation the government receives from time to time because it dares to try to entice automobile manufacturers to locate in Canada. The opposition has complained that we should not be doing that, but on the other hand they say that we are not helping Canadian industry enough. I can only say that it is part of the industrial strategy which is in place to assist Canadian business and to service Canadian markets as well as the export market.
I mentioned the Enterprise Development Board and the FBDB. Also part of the expansion concept of world trade is the multilateral trade negotiations which are going on right now. From the very beginning Canada has been a full and conscientious participator in those negotiations. We have joined in the negotiations in an attempt to widen the markets for Canadian industry, and certainly our participation has assisted in the deliberations which, I hope, will amount to a greater liberalization of trade. Rather than Canadians having preserved for themselves a market of 23 million people, they will have access to the huge market in the United States and perhaps greater access to European and Asian markets. That is part of our industrial strategy.
Participation in the multilateral trade negotiations is part of the responsibility we will be asking the EDC to assume if that trade liberalization comes about. Certainly, more goods will be moving from Canada into the world. The Export Development Corporation's role will be enlarged and more financing will be needed.
Also, my department has carried on extensive studies, what are referred to as the sector studies, of various segments of our industry to determine whether or not we can look forward to continued growth and expansion of markets in each sector in

June 28, 1978
Export Development Act
which those studies took place. They have been correlated very well with the MTN talks. I expect the sector study reports at the end of this month, and they will probably be made public in the middle of July. I am certain they will point out the potential export markets available in each one of those sectors, which ir. turn will add a greater responsibility and work load to the Export Development Corporation.
I hope people will take a look at the industrial strategy I have tried to outline and realize that the Export Development Corporation is part and parcel of it. The Enterprise Development Corporation and the Federal Business Development Bank, along with the sector studies and the MTN negotiations, are a part of it.
Much has been made of EDC loans to assist communist countries to buy Canadian goods. As 1 was sitting in my seat and listening to the hon. member for York-Simcoe mention this fact as though it were some great sin, 1 remembered the debate some 20 years ago when another government of which 1 was a member made a sale of wheat to communist China on credit. That party in those days supported the idea of making credit loans to communist countries, but apparently it has changed a great deal since then, and it is just that 1 took a long time to catch on to the change.
Opposition members complained a great deal about the loans to Cuba under the EDC. Cuba has purchased and has had fitted in many of our eastern shipyards ships for their use through the EDC, and this has meant a great deal of employment to Canada. There was also the great debate of the early sixties when the opposition supported trade with Cuba and the United States was soundly condemning the Canadian government for it. Today, if one believes that the hon. member for York-Simcoe is the spokesman for that party on questions of finance, it would follow that he would cut off all trade to communist countries and all assistance to trade with communist countries. 1 do not believe that that is the wish of the Canadian people; nor do 1 believe that western Canada or British Columbia would support that idea.
1 hope to go to China this fall, Mr. Speaker, where my department will be sponsoring a trade fair with regard to agricultural equipment, oil and gas facilities, drilling rigs and fishing gear. Certainly 1 think that we can, as 1 look to that market, expand our business there substantially. It may require more financing from the Export Development Corporation, but it will further the sale of a great many goods which I believe that country is on the threshold of needing, in the same way that the Middle East is on the threshold of buying, and is buying, a great many of the commodities which you and 1 have become accustomed to, Mr. Speaker.
I have tried to set the record straight with regard to some of the misunderstandings that have taken place in this debate. I know that hon. members want to see passage of this piece of legislation. I will not condemn the opposition too much for what they said about me personally in the debate. 1 appreciate the opportunity you have given me, Mr. Speaker. I should like to ask the minister some questions concerning the Challenger aircraft. Is there any concern in the department about the penalty clauses in the contract for the new Challenger aircraft? 1 understand that some of the contracts can be cancelled if the plane is a year behind schedule.

About $70 or $80 million in the two countries. Mr. Speaker, I am going to develop a subject which I do not think has been developed, certainly not at length, in the debate so far. It concerns the use of the Export Development Corporation, a Canadian owned
Export Development Act
Crown property, to assist Chile and the effects of that assistance. I will have an amendment to propose dealing with that subject.
May I point out first of all that Canada's investment in or contribution toward the Chilean economy, which is run, as everybody now knows, by a military junta, is very considerable. According to my information, Canada is Chile's No. 2 patron, ranking only behind the United States. 1 understand that we cannot pick and choose the different countries we would trade with or assist in trade, but in the case of Chile there are international documents that indicate it has subjected its own people to flagrant and continued violations of human rights and freedoms.
Since the military coup, a number of international bodies such as the U.N. Commission on Human Rights, the International Commission of Jurists, Amnesty International and the United Nations itself, have condemned the regime. No regime is perfect, of course. No regime can say it has never done anything against human rights. But this is one of the most extreme cases in which some sort of action is required.
In the United Nations in November 1977, when approving the report of the Economic and Social Council, the following was said:
-the Chilean people continue to be subjected to constant and flagrant violations of human rights and fundamental freedoms, to lack of adequate constitutional and judicial safeguards of their rights and liberties and to suffer assaults on the freedom and integrity of their persons, in particular by methods of systematic intimidation, including torture, disappearance of persons for political reasons, arbitrary arrest, detention, exile and deprivation of Chilean nationality.
1 leave the description of the regime to the statement issued by the United Nations which Canada supported. The policies which followed from that Canada has supported from time to time.
It is true that this regime has, on the surface at any rate, somewhat softened the methods of terror which it used. However, some of this seems to be window dressing. By replacing the state of siege it justified them, so they said, in imprisoning people without trial. They replaced the state of siege, and with a good deal of publicity then established an equally onerous state of emergency. They provided for amnesty for political prisoners but it was so conditioned that it was not available to most of those concerned. It is because of these matters, including the abolition of parliamentary government and the deprivation of trade union rights, that we are justified in saying that this is unquestionably a regime of repression, repression which is directed toward its own people.
I will go into some detail as to what assistance has come from the Export Credit Corporation. Not all of the investment or money made available to Chile from Canadian sources comes from the Export Credit Corporation. The Canadian banks have made loans and other businesses have sought to invest there, notably Falconbridge and Noranda. But nevertheless the only publicly owned or Crown operated institution which has carried on systematic assistance to this regime happens to be the Export Credit Corporation.

June 28, 1978
Export Development Act
I point out that it is not possible to loan large sums of money to secure substantial indebtedness and to enter into fairly large scale transactions without developing a vested interest in the continuation of the regime in which one is investing. That is precisely what has happened in Canada. I am sure the minister has discussed, and certainly others have discussed, the types of assistance offered by the Export Development Corporation. They include credit insurance, long-term export loans, foreign investment guarantees and surety insurance. The Export Development Corporation has expanded rapidly the loans it has made and the assistance it has given under these provisions.
A most striking illustration of the situation there occurred on October 2, 1973 a few weeks after the military coup and all the brutality surrounding it, when the EDC announced it was granting an export credit of $5 million to the Central Bank of Chile. This credit would be used to purchase six Twin Otter aircraft. These planes were for Chile's domestic airline, but military experts will confirm that these Twin Otter aircraft are extremely valuable for military purposes and particularly for the purposes of suppressing any internal trouble that might develop.
It is true that in defence of this line of credit it was said that this arrangement was negotiated before the new government came into power and while the Allende government was in office. But the loan was not announced until after the coup. Indeed, the document was not signed until January 1974, while the coup was as early as September 11. There was ample opportunity to find out exactly what was going on.
In October 1976, shortly before Canada voted condemnation of the Chilean regime at the UN, the EDC approved ten agreements covering loans, credits, insurance, foreign investment guarantees and financing to support the export sale of Canadian goods and services valued at $103 million. Chile was named as one of the six recipients. In accordance with the practice approved in a statement made by the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), it was not thought good policy to tell the people of Canada or its parliament how that loan was divided up, how much went to Chile and how much went to other countries.
The following statement in regard to the EDC foreign investment guarantee to Chile was made in 1977 to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs by the ecumenical task force on the churches and corporate responsibility:
When the EDC provides a Canadian corporation with a "political risk" insurance for a private investment in a country which consistently violates human rights, there are long-term economic and political implications. Such an investment guarantee establishes a vested interest in the "staying power" of the regime. Both the corporation making the investment, and the EDC insuring it, develop a financial interest in the stability of the recipient regime, regardless of the repressive means necessary to maintain the status quo. Thus it is possible that the EDC implicates itself, and the Canadian government, in economic relationships which maintain repressive regimes.
Again on January 18 a press release was issued announcing the approval of export credit insurance investment guarantees, surety insurance and long-term loans totalling $1,003 million to support export sales to nine countries. Chile was included
[Mr. Brcwin.J
among the list of nine recipients. The amount and type of facility exported to Chile have not been disclosed to date.
More recently, in March 1978 the Chile Economic News stated that a $14.7 million export credit was going to be extended jointly by the Bank of Montreal and the Export Development Corporation to a Chilean company, which when translated into English would be the Paper and Cardboard Manufacturing Company. The Export Development Corporation denies that such a credit has been authorized to date but admits that it might be under discussion.
Then there is the whole question of the renegotiation of debts under the so-called Paris Club in which five nations refused renegotiation of Chile's debts. Canada agreed that a renegotiation was extremely helpful to the regime.

The picture of Chile is very clear. It is a picture of a thoroughly oppressive regime bolstered by Canadian investment and guarantees, to a considerable extent financed by a Canadian Crown corporation. That is wrong. A former minister of finance, John Turner, said when this matter was discussed that the question of the morality of the regime should be discussed by other fora. In other words, he advocated a policy whereby you condemn something in the United Nations and then you acquiesce and strengthen it in practical actions.
I propose to move an amendment. Perhaps I can read it now.
I am afraid the hon. member will not find it very exciting. However, it complies with the rules, I believe. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That all the words after the word "that" be deleted and that the following words be substituted therefor:
"Bill C-36 be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs for the purpose of reconsidering clauses 2 and 3 thereof."
The purpose behind the amendment is to give the committee an opportunity to consider the matters which I have raised. The present bill provides for the extension of further credits and further financial assistance. It in no way limits where they shall go. It in no way complies with the policy of the United Nations. Clauses 2 and 3, if reconsidered, could be amended so as to prohibit these loans.
One does not like to call the government of one's own country hypocritical. I have tried to figure out what hypocritical means. It means somebody who talks one way, who pronounces noble sentiments in one breath, but whose actions totally belie what he has said.

June 28, 1978

When you have a policy of using our Crown corporations and money secured from Canadian people to bolster a regime that is repressive, depressing all the people of Chile, the Canadian people might like to know how you determine that country should be banned. I say it is very simple. The Commissioner of Human Rights should be asked to secure information from organizations such as the United Nations and Amnesty International and to say that there is evidence that this is a regime which not incidentally but systematically and continuously breaches human rights. If the House accepts this amendment and the committee sees fit to deal with it in the way I have suggested, we will at least be making our actions fit in with our professions. I believe the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at one time said we should do that, and I agree.
Hypocrisy is not an attractive thing. It is certainly not attractive to other countries we deal with and it should not be attractive to us. I hope the House will decide to take some action on this motion.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this third reading debate and, in the process, deal with some of the comments made by the minister this afternoon.
When I first came to Canada, I recognized that this is a country which in many instances is a developed country but at the same time is a developing country. In effect, it has much of the characteristics of the third world.
Exports from this country have predominantly been raw or semi-processed goods. While we in this party have no quarrel with the aims of the Export Development Corporation in assisting and facilitating the export of finished products, in Canada's present state of development there are certain areas in which the EDC involves itself which do not serve the best interests of Canada. This is what we have been arguing in committee and it has been exemplified in many parts of the country.
When I moved from St. Catharines in southern Ontario to the Sudbury basin, I asked why the people there take nickel and copper out of the ground, process it to a semi-processed state in pellet form, put it in barrels and ship it to the United States for final processing and finishing into a product, or ship it abroad to Norway or Wales for final processing. Then later on we buy back the finished product. These are questions we must ask ourselves.
When the minister speaks to selected audiences, as he spoke the other day to the Bankers Association, he does not talk to people at the grass roots. He does not face the people to answer the questions which are on their lips. That first question of mine is one of them.
Another is this: Why not carry out research to find new uses of nickel and copper? This is 1978. They have been mining the stuff for well over 60 years now, yet the industry still lacks an infrastructure. Why should it be necessary for us to import rolled nickel for the use of the Royal Canadian Mint? Why
Export Development Act
should we buy back at a high price material which was originally produced here in Thompson, Manitoba? Why is it that we produce pulp from the forests of this country and ship it out in a semi-processed state, buying back the finished products from Europe and the United States? We have the resources and the manpower right here. With one million people unemployed why should we import these finished products? Take any resource sector you like, the same question must be asked.
Another important factor in this equation is the extent of the foreign ownership of our industries. So much of our industry is locked into the multinational web. Take, for example, Inco and Falconbridge. These companies mine nickel and copper in the Sudbury basin but they have expanded to other parts of the world. Inco has to be flexible and at certain times it might be more appropriate for the company to increase production in Guatemala or Indonesia. It is more convenient to carry out research and development in the country of the parent company. In the case of Falconbridge and Inco it is important that research and development be done in the United States, so that if any untoward political event occurred in Canada the technology resides with the parent company. Much of Canada's trading pattern is related to this important aspect. We find subsidiaries of parent companies in other countries being forbidden to bid against the parent company in world markets.
What we are seeing now is the superimposing of the Export Development Corporation on this picture. We do not quarrel with EDC assisting, for example, Northern Telecom to put in place a telecommunications system in Algeria or Saudi Arabia. This involves finished products and such projects improve the quality of life in the countries receiving them. They are probably sponsored by the governments concerned.
On the other hand, there are certain sectors in which the corporation should bear in mind the long-term interests of Canada in terms of jobs and economic advantage. It is not the short term the corporation should be considering but, rather, the long term. I have in mind the loans made to Inco, the insurance offered to Superior Oil in the Dominican Republic, the loan to the Bear Island Paper Company in Virginia. EDC should ask itself: What will be the net effect down the line of our decisions on employment in Canada? This is an extremely important factor and one which is missing in the corporation's appraisal of applications for loans.
We are told by ministers and others that if these developments are going ahead anyway we should join in and get our piece of the action. I am not convinced that this position is a sound one to take. I have looked at the rules governing an agency comparable to EDC, the EX-IM Bank which operates under an act of the United States government, and it is clearly stated that the EX-IM Bank must consider the long term effect of its decisions on employment in the United States. It was on the basis of this clause that the bank turned down the application for a loan to establish a steel plant in Trinidad; it was evident that in the long term the establishment of such a
