plant would have an adverse effect on employment in the United States.
The argument has been advanced that by granting these loans we were somehow or other improving the quality of life in countries abroad, for example, in Indonesia or Guatemala. But the question workers in the Sudbury basin ask when they receive lay-off notices and hear on the news that EDC has lent an Inco subsidiary millions of dollars to go to Guatemala or Indonesia is this: Why cannot that sort of money be used as venture capital in Sudbury so that we can diversify the nickel and related industries? Why cannot we develop new uses for copper and nickel? We are talking now in terms of $77 million-the minister himself rounded it off at $80 million. Suppose that sum was matched, $80 million from the federal government and $80 million from the province. Action on these lines ought to be part of an industrial strategy.
I do not understand how EDC can be following its present course at a time when the nickel industry in this country is still not fully integrated, at a time when the industry is being challenged by supplies of nickel from Guatemala and Indonesia. Mr. Speaker, we are not improving the quality of life for workers in Guatemala and Indonesia. The technology resides with Inco, not with the people of those countries.
When the company decides to move out of Guatemala for one reason or another, or when the resource is exhausted because it has been high graded, no technology will be left with the people. So they really have no control over development for the benefit of future generations. I think we have to keep that in mind. That is the kind of propaganda we have been getting from the minister. He says that somehow we are improving the lives and living standards of these people. It is all short term. It is short term for Guatemala as well as for Canada.
It is not by accident that we end up supporting and lending money to corporations like Inco in places like Guatemala, Indonesia and The Philippines. These are all countries with very repressive dictatorships. Amnesty International has documented the fact that over 50,000 political prisoners are in Indonesian jails without trial. It is not by accident that we are now lending $22 million to develop a pulp and paper industry in Chile, which has one of the most repressive regimes ever seen in the western world. Let us keep in mind that that junta overthrew the legally elected democratic government of Salvador Allende. Today is the anniversary of Salvador Allende's birth, and I think it is inappropriate that through the Export Development Corporation this government is strengthening a junta which has denied democracy in a Latin American country which had a long history of democratic government.
This is a hypocritical performance on the part of this government. On the one hand we condemn the loss of democratic freedom in one part of the world, and on the other we do not bat an eye when the same thing is done in our own back yard. The Export Development Corporation is moving in to strengthen and develop an industry in Chile. People are asking

why we are putting that kind of money into an industry which we ourselves have not fully integrated and modernized.
We are helping to develop a modern pulp and paper plant in Virginia. The minister mentioned that. He said it will be a modern plant which will make us more competitive in the development of technology. However, we have not built into our own pulp and paper industry the infrastructure and diversification which would allow the industry to be competitive on the world market. We still have pulp and paper plants which are decrepit. Companies have refused to modernize their plants here, yet they borrow taxpayers' money to modernize abroad. There was a perfect example of that in Temis-camingue, Quebec where an American multinational headquartered in New York closed its plant because it was not modern. The company left the people in that community high and dry. Governments had to come to the rescue.
It seems to me we are always picking up the pieces after the fact. I wish we would start moving in where there are profits for a change instead of subsidizing losses. Parts of the MacMillan Bloedel operation in Vancouver need to be modernized if the company is to be competitive, but what does the EDC do? I heard in committee that $75,000 was spent breaking out the booze last year to celebrate those fancy contracts which were signed. It makes the people in the Sudbury Basin really happy to know that $75,000 was spent to entertain.
Some might think that these companies are doing us a favour, but we are doing them a favour because we are giving them long-term loans at very favourable rates of interest, considering those long terms. The board of directors of the EDC contains not one worker or representative of workers. Who is on the board of directors of the EDC? Mr. MacDonald is the president. He was a big-wig in the Department of Supply and Services. Now he is the big president. Then there is Mr. Bouey, Governor of the Bank of Canada. Then there is Mr. Burns, who is a Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Then there is Mr. Dupuy, President of CIDA, Mr. Godwin, President of Seismic Service, and Mr. Gotlieb, Under-Secretary of State for External Affairs. Then there is Mr. Lavoie, President and General Manager of Credit Fonder, and Mr. Osbaldeston, a Deputy Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. There is Mr. Shoyama, Deputy Minister of Finance, Mr. Ross, President of Swan Wooster Engineering Company Limited, and Mr. Stuart, President and General Manager of the Electrolyser Corporation Limited. Now Mr. Nickerson of the company Nickerson and Sons of North Sydney has been added.
Here are these boys breaking out the champagne to celebrate these contracts. What are the workers doing? They are breaking out the 7-Up as they get their lay-off notices because their plants have to close down for seven or eight weeks. They have to go on unemployment insurance and collect from the taxpayers of this country. This cabal, it seems, has no concept of what it is like to be unemployed. I think they should spend a year on unemployment insurance with no other income so that they can get the feel of it. Let them drink 7-Up rather than the Andres Baby Duck or whatever. They probably had imported
June 28, 1978

champagne anyway, $75,000 worth of the sparkling stuff. I suppose they were drinking champagne and eating those little things called hors-d'oeuvres.
Instead of going up to the big bash for the Bankers Association of the Sudbury basin and speaking to those people, I wish the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce had gone down to the union hall and answered workers' questions. Perhaps he might then have been glad that capital punishment has been abolished. In an industry so sensitive to development as the nickel industry, people ask why we have this kind of money to lend abroad.
The minister made light of the fact that only $80 million in a $900 million operation was involved. Well, $80 million is not a small amount, and every $80 million counts. For example, it was $80 million for the Inco operations in Guatemala and Indonesia. It was about $40 million for Alcan. There is another perfect example. Alcan closed down the community of St. Lawrence. Every single person in that community was put out of work. The community became a ghost town. With this federal Liberal government in power ghost towns have been created across northern Ontario and across the country. Alcan closed down the community of St. Lawrence, and what is the EDC doing? It is lending Alcan about $40 million to run off to Ireland to build a refinery. People wonder why the EDC is doing these things, and the answer does not come. We keep getting the answer that if we do not put the money there, the project would go ahead anyway, so we get our piece of the action.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that there are better places to put our money. We could take the $1 billion EDC is asking for and invest it in the industrial development of areas such as the Sudbury basin or Cape Breton, and spend $500 million to modernize the steel plant there so that the community could compete with steel products in the world-never mind building a steel plant in the eastern United States. We need to spend that money on developing the planning and processing operation of the fish we catch off the east coast. We are still sending semi-processed fish to the United States to be canned and sold there. What we should do is to spend that money on modernizing and extending our fish plants so that we can have an integrated operation here. This is our strength. Why is it that in as fragile an economy as ours in terms of the resource sector we are investing billions of dollars on short-term projects when in fact we should be investing that money on long-term projects?
When 1 criticized the EDC loan, Inco wrote to me and said that the loan had created 4,000 man-years of work as a result of the subcontracts that were given out. We have to keep that in perspective and remember that those man-years were taken up mostly by Inco workers, Inco top brass people who were sent down to Guatemala and Indonesia. The loan did not create any new employment but was taken up by their fulltime employees. Only the other day I received the passport of one of them who was going to Indonesia.

The minister spoke about expertise. We do not have expertise in terms of research and development. It needs to be developed. We do not have the expertise to create new products from copper or nickel. It needs to be developed. If the minister were to say honestly to EDC: "We will look at long-term jobs, we will look at the sectors to which we will lend that money", 1 would have no objection or quarrel with that. 1 would not object to having the money go to, say, the development of a telecommunications system in Algeria, or to putting it in the building of new railway lines in Mexico so that we could sell them our railway stock. But when it comes to the resource sector, we have not developed the infrastructure around it, so it is stupid to create employment outside Canada instead of investing our money in research and development for the development of rolling mills for copper and nickel in this country, for example. That is where the misplaced emphasis is. There is a great emphasis on short-term, high technology jobs, whereas there are other opportunities in the long term.
Some government members sit over there like a bunch of scarecrows putting up five fingers. I do not know what it means. They can make all the fun they want, but they did not get an unemployment or lay-off notice in October. They will get one at the next election.
These are the concerns that the people have. The minister said that we need an industrial strategy. I agree we need an industrial strategy, but it should be co-ordinated.

No, they do not look down the line and they do not see the threat from ocean floor mining. The advent of ocean floor mining is posing a threat to our nickel and copper industries. The minister says that our contribution is only $77 million of $900 million. If that amount of money were properly and judiciously used in Canada, it would go a long way toward diversifying our economy. That is why we have employment problems in Canada. The minister is making loans through EDC which create short-term jobs, while the large multinational corporations are laying off employees in the hinterland. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) referred to the question of morality involved with EDC loans. The government set out guidelines regarding the behaviour of Canadian corporations doing business with South Africa. EDC has indicated that its men have been removed from Cape Town, South Africa; but if a Canadian company which does business in South Africa applies for an EDC loan, there is no question at all, the loan is granted. In effect, we are supporting the regime in South Africa.
This has nothing to do with politics. It concerns human realization. The South African government is based on the philosophy that black men and white men are not equal, that the white men are better. The government issues guidelines but does not forbid Canadian Crown corporations making loans to corporations which do business in South Africa.
Also EDC indicated that it does not do business with Rhodesia because Great Britain has said that the Rhodesian government is illegal. In fact, that country was put out of the Commonwealth, as was South Africa. During the time when
the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) was the prime minister of this country, South Africa was put out of the Commonwealth because of its racist policies, philosophy and behaviour. The government should display some backbone and indicate that Canada does not aspire to the philosophy that one race is better than another. This government should take that position. It took a similar position in respect of Taiwan for political reasons. Why would the government not take that position regarding South Africa on the basis of common decency and humanity?
Also the hon. member for Greenwood mentioned the strengthening of the Chilean and Argentinian regimes. It was a government guarantee which put $126 million into the pockets of the Argentian government for the purchase of a Candu reactor. We are well aware of the spin-off effects of that. Not only are regimes strengthened, but secrecy surrounds the operations of EDC. It would be eminently wise if this corporation was brought before a standing committee of the House on a regular basis in order to question it on the basis of its regulations respecting loans.
In closing, I do not have any disagreement with the basic premise of EDC. I see a need for that corporation in respect of the exporting of finished Canadian products. In the area of resource development, until we are on the path of placing ourselves in a competitive position at home, then it is stupid and insensitive to help multinational corporations develop and integrate more modern facilities in other parts of the world. Oftentimes this occurs in very developed countries such as the United States. That is being very insensitive to the needs of Canadians.
Basically that is my quarrel. EDC should adopt a hands off policy respecting the resource sector. If there is money for investment, we should develop our resource sector first. We should modernize it, integrate it and make it competitive at home. After that has been accomplished, then Inco can develop a plant in Indonesia, Guatemala or wherever. That would result in Canadian workers having a better chance of maintaining their long-term employment.
One should consider that problem as well as the question of morality, but the crux of the problem is in the area of long-term effect on Canadian jobs. Instead of receiving lay-off notices, the people at the grass roots level will respond. When they see pictures of the president of EDC and the boys from Falconbridge in the newspapers breaking open champagne, enjoying lobster and having a whale of a good time-
Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue with unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) left me a

June 28, 1978

few minutes between now and six o'clock to make a few comments. At the outset I should like to indicate that I have listened to much of this debate. I am pleased that it has gone on for some period of time, and that it has been given some airing. It provides the Canadian public with an opportunity to be concerned about many of the things EDC has been doing.
EDC has done three things. It has assisted companies to develop certain techniques in this country for export, which is all to the good. This has helped these Canadian companies establish international reputations. They are able to sell products in countries which are having difficulties. Hopefully those countries will repay us. If they cannot give us the money back, at least they can provide us with markets. That segment of EDC is very valuable, and we support it.
The other two segments cannot be explained easily to the general public. The hon. member for Nickel Belt dealt with one in his closing remarks. What has happened to the resource industry of this country when we allow companies to take their money, money which they make in this country from natural resources, into another country? We not only allow them to do that which is prohibited in most other countries, but the Canadian government assists them, although there is very little chance of any gain and a good chance of eliminating our own markets.
Members have mentioned the pulp and paper industry and the mining resource industry. In both areas there is no justification for allowing loans to be made to industry that will be in direct competition with the industries of this country. There are other areas we can develop in other countries that are not competitive with Canadian industries. We should develop our own industry. The minister comes from an area where we have been developing our own industry for a long time, and that is the industry of cereal production.
We have given loans to people to buy our products through EDC and to develop in their own countries an agricultural potential as well because we know that we are able to out-com-pete those countries. We should not, however, allow an unfair advantage to develop in industries such as gold, silver, nickel, magnesium and many other commodities which come from deep sea mining because it will be at the expense of our own industry if that foreign industry can develop and compete in world markets.
I think that it would be wise for the House to give some consideration to the CIA operation we have been supporting in Canada under the guise of other agencies. EDC is really one of the branches of our Canadian CIA. We provide aid to some countries that are not economically viable and from which we have no chance of getting our money back. We are simply making that loan in a political sense to governments that we would not, under any circumstances, as Canadian citizens support if we understood the policies of those governments.
When we give aid to countries in Africa we should know what kind of country we are giving that aid to and who will be receiving the benefits. There was a book recently previewed on television by a CIA agent from the United States who did an
Export Development Act
expose on his experiences heading up the CIA in Angola, where that organization was running an army and in effect trying to maintain the status quo by covert acts. The Canadian public does not want this to happen with the EDC.
I think, therefore, that we should support this amendment which in effect would send this bill back to committee to consider some of the countries and companies to which we are providing aid today, as well as some of the aspirations and wishes to the Canadian public who are really never considered in many of these giveaway programs.
I, like the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), sometimes get annoyed when I see a number of people indicating that if we are going to continue talking we will interrupt their supper hour and that it behooves me to sit down so that they may have a lot of time for their supper.
That's dinner.

Dinner, supper; to me supper, to you dinner. I come from an old Canadian family where we had breakfast, lunch and then supper. If some other people come from the English aristocracy, that is perfectly all right and they can call it what they wish. I do not want to get sidetracked, but I know that you will bring me back to the subject if I get the least bit off it, Mr. Speaker, we did not really stop for tea in those days.
I would like members of this House to consider the wishes of the Canadian public who do not want to see our natural resource industries put out of business and all our communities placed in jeopardy because we provide loans to people which give them a competitive advantage over our own industries. Nor do Canadians want to provide the tyrants of South America, Africa and any other country operated by such governments with the kind of support they could receive under the EDC. I ask that hon. members reconsider this bill and support the amendment.
Is the House ready for the question?
Question.
The question is on the amendment. Is it the pleasure of the House to adopt the said motion?
Agreed.
No.
All those in favour will please say yea.
Yea.

Nay.
